## What this exercise is

Exercises 1--3 ran on data that shipped inside an R package. This one
does not. You will work with **real surveillance data** --- COVID-19
deaths in the 67 counties of Pennsylvania --- and assemble the analysis
dataset yourself, the way you would in a health department: a table of
counts from one source, county boundaries from another, and a join
between them that has to be checked rather than trusted.

From there the exercise follows the sequence of the last two weeks:

1.  join and project the data;
2.  compute crude rates, **expected counts**, and the **standardized
    mortality ratio (SMR)**;
3.  map the SMR honestly --- which, for a ratio, is not the same as
    mapping a rate;
4.  build a spatial weights matrix and ask, with **global Moran's I**,
    whether the SMRs are spatially structured or could plausibly be
    arranged at random.

It is worth 17.5 points and carries more weight than the first two
exercises. Start early: Part A is where most of the unexpected problems
will be.

## The data

**Counts.** `pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv` is posted on Course Site. It is a
subset of the **Johns Hopkins University CSSE COVID-19 Data Repository**
(`time_series_covid19_deaths_US.csv`), the source behind the JHU
dashboard that was the most widely used COVID-19 tracker in the United
States until the project stopped updating in March 2023. The repository
compiles counts reported by state health departments --- here, the
Pennsylvania Department of Health --- and attributes deaths to the
county of residence.

| Column | Meaning |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `UID`, `FIPS` | JHU identifier; county FIPS code |
| `Admin2` | County name |
| `Province_State` | State |
| `Population` | County population (U.S. Census Bureau 2019 estimate, as carried in the JHU file) |
| `deaths_2020` | Cumulative COVID-19 deaths reported through December 31, 2020 |

Cite the source in your document as: Dong, E., Du, H., & Gardner, L.
(2020). An interactive web-based dashboard to track COVID-19 in real
time. *The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 20*(5), 533--534, together with
the repository URL: <https://github.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19>.

**Boundaries.** County polygons come from the U.S. Census Bureau's
**cartographic boundary files**, downloaded inside your document with
the `tigris` package. Install it once, in the console ---
`install.packages(c("tigris", "ggrepel"))` --- not inside the document.

::: callout-note
## Why 2020

Calendar year 2020 is the first pandemic year and the period before
vaccines were available. Treat the population as the population at risk
for one year.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(leaflet)
library(spdep)
library(ggrepel)            # non-overlapping labels
library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)   # download once, then reuse

covid <- read_csv("pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv")
pa    <- counties(state = "PA", cb = TRUE, year = 2020)
```

## Part A --- Assemble the dataset (3 points)

1.  Inspect both objects. How many rows does `covid` have, and how many
    polygons does `pa` have? The two numbers differ. Find the rows
    responsible and say in one sentence what they are and why they
    cannot be mapped. Covid has 69 rows and pa has 67 polygons. The rows
    responsible are "Out of PA" and "Unassigned." These categories
    represent deaths that were not assigned to a specific county or
    happened outside of Pennsylvania' 67 counties, so they cannot be
    mapped in the state.

2.  Identify the column in each object that identifies a county. Show
    what the values look like in each, and say why they will not match
    as they stand. In 'pa' GEOID identifies each county as a 5 digit
    identifier, with the first 2 values representing the state (42 for
    PA), and the next representing the county. For example, 42095
    represents Northampton County, where Lehigh University is located.
    In 'covid' FIPS represents each county. FIPS are government issued
    numerical identifiers that represent geographic areas, and they
    contain the same numbers as the GEOID column in PA. For example,
    Northampton county is the five digit identifier 42095. The reason
    the two columns do not match despite visually looking the same is
    how they are kept within the data set. The 'covid' FIPS data is
    numerical, while the 'pa' GEOID data is stored as a string.

3.  Create a join key in `covid` that matches the one in `pa`, then
    **join the counts onto the polygons**. Show, with code, that every
    one of the 67 counties received a count --- do not just look at the
    map. To show that all 67 counties received a count, I checked that
    there were no "NA" indicating something went wrong. I also checked
    that the data had 67 rows, showing no counties were dropped and that
    nothing had been duplicated.

4.  In two or three sentences: why join the table onto the polygons
    (`left_join(pa, covid)`) rather than the other way around, and what
    would an **inner** join have hidden from you if the key had been
    only partly wrong? A join decides which rows of a table survive,
    with a left join keeping all of the rows from 'pa' and adding on
    matching rows from 'covid.' Because the 67 polygons are what we are
    studying, those must go in the left surviving table, ensuring all
    come through the join. A failed match would show up as NA, which is
    detectable, while the reverse would include all 69 rows of 'covid,'
    including the "Out of PA" and "Unassigned" rows. An inner join on
    the other hand keeps only the rows that match on both tables which
    could be an issue if there was a formatting problem in the data,
    making it seem like some of the counties had no match, because they
    would be dropped from the table. No NAs would appear so that check
    would be pointless. Essentially, an inner join could cause problems
    silently, making me unaware there is something wrong in the data.

::: callout-tip
Run the obvious join first,
`left_join(pa, covid, by = c("GEOID" = "FIPS"))`, and read the error
message carefully. It tells you exactly what is wrong. A FIPS code is an
**identifier**, not a number: `42001` and `42001.0` are the same number
but not the same identifier, and a county such as `01001` in Alabama
would lose its leading zero.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: a-starter

# A1
nrow(covid); nrow(pa)

#rows in the table with no polygon to go to (names are good enough to look) #remove rows with no attachable polygons
anti_join(covid, st_drop_geometry(pa), by = c("Admin2" = "NAME"))

# A2 -- what type is each key?
str(covid$FIPS)
str(pa$GEOID)

# A3 -- a five-character, zero-padded text key #make sure data are integers
covid <- covid |>
 mutate(GEOID = sprintf("%05d", as.integer(FIPS)))

pa_covid <- pa |>
 left_join(covid, by = "GEOID")

#left_join(pa, covid, by = c("GEOID" = "FIPS"))

# prove the join worked
sum(is.na(pa_covid$deaths_2020))
nrow(pa_covid)
anyDuplicated(pa_covid$GEOID)
```

## Part B --- Coordinate reference system (1.5 points)

1.  What CRS do the Census boundaries arrive in? Geographic or
    projected? The Census boundaries arrive in NAD83, aka. the North
    American Datum of 1983 (EPSG:4269), which is longitude and latitude
    and is therefore geographic; this is confirmed in the return of
    `st_is_longlat(pa_covid` as TRUE.

2.  Transform `pa_covid` to a **projected** CRS appropriate for the
    whole state, and state its EPSG code. Pennsylvania is split between
    two State Plane zones (North and South) and two UTM zones, so the
    obvious choices each cover only part of the state --- say what you
    chose and why it is acceptable for a statewide map. I have chosen to
    use EPSG code EPSG:5070 which uses the Albers Equal Area Conic map
    projection. I chose it because preserves area proportion across the
    whole map and at a state level does not cause much distortion. It
    can cause distortion on local levels, but because we are looking at
    the whole of PA it should be minimally distorted. This avoids the
    issue of the state being split in two by the State PLane zones or
    the UTM zones.

3.  One sentence: which of the operations in this exercise actually
    depend on the projection, and which do not?
    The things that need the geometry's shape or area depend on the projection.  In this exercise that includes the static maps and the leaflet map (which uses long/lat).  Things such as crude rates, expected counts, SMR, Moran's I, CI, and queen contiguity do not.



### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: b-starter

st_crs(pa_covid)$input
st_crs(pa_covid)$epsg #returns EPSG number
st_is_longlat(pa_covid) #TRUE= geographic

pa_covid <- st_transform(pa_covid, crs="EPSG:5070") #transforms from EPSG:4269 to EPSG:5070
st_is_longlat(pa_covid) #FALSE = projected
```

## Part C --- Counts, rates, expected counts, and the SMR (4.5 points)

1.  Compute the **crude COVID-19 mortality rate per 100,000** for 2020
    in every county. Report the three highest and three lowest. Highest
    Crude Mortality Rates (high-low):

    1.  Mifflin County: 257.9219
    2.  Northumberland County: 248.7809
    3.  Bedford County: 196.2913 Lowest Crude Mortality Rates
        (low-high):
    4.  Wayne County: 35.04605
    5.  Forest County: 41.39644
    6.  Greene County: 41.39872

2.  Make two quick static maps with `ggplot2`, placed side by side: the
    **number of deaths** as **proportional symbols**, and the **crude
    rate** as a choropleth with a sequential, colour-blind-safe palette.
    Both need a legend title with units. In two or three sentences: why
    is a count shown with symbols rather than a choropleth, which
    counties stand out on each map, and why do the two maps tell
    different stories? The counts are shown as symbols so that the size
    actually represents something. If they were in a choropleth, it
    could look like visually that counties that are larger had higher
    counts, when in actuality they do not. Keeping them as symbols
    separates the size of the county with the size of the count
    visually. On the count map the counties of Philadelphia, Delaware,
    Montgomery, and Bucks stand out because they are large circles and
    close together and Allegheny stands out because it appears to have a
    larger count then surrounding counties. On the choropleth map
    Mifflin and Northumberland stand out because they are the darkest,
    indicating the largest crude rates. These maps tell different
    stories because the crude rate takes the large populations of
    counties such as Philadelphia into account, whereas the count map
    does not, so it shows larger numbers in more populous counties.

3.  Compute the **statewide reference rate**
    $r = \sum_i O_i / \sum_i P_i$, and from it the **expected count** in
    each county, $E_i = r \times P_i$. Show that
    $\sum_i E_i = \sum_i O_i$ and explain in one sentence why this must
    be so. Statewide reference rate = 125.2149 deaths per 100,000
    population `sum(pa_covid$E); sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020)` are equal.
    The expected rate is calculated using the statewide reference rate
    times the population, and because we are looking at deaths on a
    state level, these are equal. Essentially:
    $r = \sum_i O_i / \sum_i P_i$ can also be worded
    $\sum_i O_i  = r * \sum_i P_i$ and $E_i = r \times P_i$ so therefore
    $\sum_i E_i = \sum_i O_i$.

4.  Compute the **SMR**, $O_i / E_i$.

    a.  Interpret the SMR of one county of your choice in a full
        sentence a county commissioner could understand. For Northampton
        county the Standardized Mortality Ratio was 1.13, meaning that
        Northampton county had 13% more deaths than expected compared to
        the statewide rate: 431 deaths were observed compared to the
        expected about 382 deaths for if the county had experienced the
        same rates as PA as a whole.

    b.  Divide each county's crude rate by the statewide rate and
        compare with the SMR. Explain why they are identical here, and
        what $E_i$ would have to take into account for the two to
        differ. *(This is where we are going later in the semester.)*
        The new rate and the SMR are the same because:
        $New Rate = Crude Rate/r = (O_i /P_i)/r = O_i /(P_i * r) = O_i /E_i = SMR$
        If $E_i$ took into account a factor such as age or something
        else that changes how vulnerable a people are to dying of COVID,
        that could make them differ, as it is currently based on
        population alone. If one county had a much older overall
        population then these could differ because they would have a
        much higher expected count of death because older people have a
        higher risk of dying from COVID and expected counts could be
        built off of age-specific reference rates.

5.  Compute an exact **95% confidence interval** for every SMR (formula
    below). Compare the intervals for the two or three counties with the
    **fewest** deaths with those of the counties with the **highest**
    SMRs. In three or four sentences: what does this tell you about the
    extreme values on an SMR map?
    The CI intervals for the counties with the fewest deaths were between 0.74-1.64 away from eachother.  The CI intervals for the counties with the highest SMR were between 0.38-0.91 away from eachother.  These numbers were calculated by subtracting the lower CI number from the higher CI number, and are simply a representation of how wide of an interval the CI has.  The range of CI intervals for the counties with the fewest deaths was much larger than the rand for the counties with the highest SMR.  This shows that for low count counties, the SMRs are unstable.  This is confirmed by 4 out fo the 5 fewest death counties CI interval crossing through 1, showing that they are not statistically significant.  The counties with the highest SMR's however, all had intervals that excluded 1.  This says that when counts are small, extreme values appear by chance and can mean little.

::: callout-note
## Where the confidence interval comes from

Treat the expected count $E$ as a fixed constant and the observed count
as Poisson, $O \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)$ with
$\mu = \text{SMR} \times E$. We first find an exact 95% interval for
$\mu$ and then divide both ends by $E$.

The lower bound $\mu_L$ is the value of $\mu$ at which observing $O$
**or more** deaths has probability 0.025; the upper bound $\mu_U$ is the
value at which observing $O$ **or fewer** has probability 0.025. Because
of the link between the Poisson and chi-square distributions, both have
a closed form:

$$\mu_L = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.025,\;2O}, \qquad
\mu_U = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.975,\;2(O+1)} .$$

Dividing by $E$ gives the interval for the SMR:

$$\left[\ \frac{\chi^2_{0.025,\,2O}}{2E}\ ,\ \ \frac{\chi^2_{0.975,\,2(O+1)}}{2E}\ \right].$$

The upper bound uses $2(O+1)$ degrees of freedom and the lower bound
$2O$; that asymmetry is what keeps the interval exact when counts are
small. When $O = 0$ the lower bound is 0.

**Worked example.** A county with $O = 4$ and $E = 5.57$ has SMR
$= 0.72$ and

``` r
qchisq(0.025, 2 * 4)       / (2 * 5.57)   # 0.20
qchisq(0.975, 2 * (4 + 1)) / (2 * 5.57)   # 1.84
poisson.test(4, T = 5.57)$conf.int        # same interval: E acts as the "time base"
```

The familiar normal approximation,
$\text{SMR} \times \exp(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{O})$, works for counties with
many deaths but breaks down for the smallest ones --- which are exactly
the counties this question is about --- and is undefined when $O = 0$.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: c-starter

# C1
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(crude_rate = 100000 * deaths_2020 / Population)

#find 3 highest crude rates
three_highest <- pa_covid[order(pa_covid$crude_rate, decreasing = TRUE), ][1:3, ]
print(three_highest)

#find 3 lowest crude rates
three_lowest <- pa_covid[order(pa_covid$crude_rate, decreasing = FALSE), ][1:3, ]
print(three_lowest)

# C2 -- counts as proportional symbols
pts <- st_point_on_surface(pa_covid)        # one point inside each county

p_count <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = pa_covid, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = pts, aes(size = deaths_2020),
          shape = 21, fill = "firebrick", colour = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 14, name = "Deaths in 2020 (count)") +   # area proportional to count
  labs(title = "COVID Deaths in 2020") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(
    size = guide_legend(
      title.position = "top"))

# rates as a choropleth

p_rate <- ggplot(pa_covid) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = crude_rate), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = "Death Rate per 100,000 Population") +
  labs(title = "Crude Mortality Rate for COVID Deaths in 2020") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(
    fill = guide_colourbar(title.position = "top"))

p_count + p_rate

# C3 -- one number for the whole state
r <- sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020) / sum(pa_covid$Population)
r * 100000                         # per 100,000

pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(E = r * Population)

sum(pa_covid$E); sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020)

# C4
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(SMR = deaths_2020/E)

summary(pa_covid$SMR)

#county crude rate divided by the statewide rate
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(crude_v_state = crude_rate/(r*100000))

#should be TRUE
all.equal(pa_covid$SMR, pa_covid$crude_v_state)

# C5 -- exact Poisson interval
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(SMR_lo = qchisq(0.025, 2 * deaths_2020) / (2 * E),
         SMR_hi = qchisq(0.975, 2 * (deaths_2020 + 1)) / (2 * E))

#length of CI
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(CI_length = SMR_hi - SMR_lo)

#compare counties with fewest deaths
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(deaths_2020) |>
  select(NAME, Population, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi, CI_length) |>
  head(5)

#compare counties with highest SMR
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(SMR)) |>
  select(NAME, Population, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi, CI_length) |>
  head(5)
```

## Part D --- Mapping a ratio (3.5 points)

In Exercise 1 a sequential palette was the right choice for a rate. An
SMR is different: it is a ratio with a **meaningful reference value of
1**, and it is **multiplicative** --- an SMR of 2 is as far above
expected as 0.5 is below it.

1.  Map the SMR as an interactive **`leaflet`** map with a **diverging
    palette centred on 1** and **class breaks you set yourself**. Choose
    breaks that are symmetric on the ratio scale, and make the class
    around 1 read as "about as expected". Justify the palette and the
    breaks in three or four sentences.
    I chose the breaks based on the idea that SMR is multiplicative.  Zero-0.5 is less than half of expected  deaths, 0.5-0.67 is well below expected deaths, 0.67-0.8 is below expected deaths, 0.8 to 1.25 range represents about what is expected for deaths, 1.25-1.5 represents a bit above expected deaths, 1.5-2 is well above expected deaths, and 2 and up is more than double expected deaths.  The red blue palette shows this as well, with darker blues deepening to show less than expected deaths, closer to white showing expected deaths, and deeper reds showing more than expected deaths. It is also color blind safe.  These choices both work together to show what is important: which direction a county diverges from the reference value of 1.  That is important because it represents if the county is doing better or worse than expected, and can indicate what counties may need interventions. 
    
2.  Your SMR map meets the standards from Exercise 1 --- legend title
    with units or meaning, thin boundaries, colour-blind-safe palette
    --- and in addition:
    - a **source line** on the map naming the data and the year;
    - a **popup** for each county giving the observed and expected
      deaths, the SMR, and its 95% interval from C5. This is what makes
      an interactive map worth having: the reader can check how much
      evidence stands behind a colour.

::: callout-warning
## `leaflet` wants longitude and latitude

Web maps are drawn on a Web Mercator basemap and expect coordinates in
**EPSG:4326**. Your `pa_covid` is now projected (Part B), so give
`leaflet` a transformed **copy**, `st_transform(pa_covid, 4326)`, and
keep the projected object for everything else. Handing it projected
coordinates is the most common reason for a blank `leaflet` map.
:::

::: callout-tip
## What earns full marks here

Breaks that follow from what an SMR *means*, not from the distribution
of the values. A student who can explain why 0.67 and 1.5 belong in the
same break set understands the variable.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: d-starter

pa_wgs <- st_transform(pa_covid, 4326)      # leaflet needs lon/lat

# D1 -- breaks symmetric on the ratio scale: 1/x and x
brks <- c(0, 0.5, 0.67, 0.8, 1.25, 1.5, 2, Inf) #0, 1/2, 1/1.5, 1/1.25, 1.25, 1.5, 2

pal <- colorBin("RdBu", domain = pa_wgs$SMR, bins = brks,
                reverse = TRUE)             # red = high

leaflet(pa_wgs) |>
  addTiles() |>                               # OpenStreetMap basemap
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(SMR), fillOpacity = 0.8,
    color = "white", weight = 0.6,          # thin boundaries
    label = ~NAME,                          # shown on hover
    popup = ~sprintf("<b>%s County</b><br>Observed: %d<br>Expected: %.1f<br>SMR: %.2f (95%% CI %.2f-%.2f)",
                     NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi),
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(weight = 2, color = "black",
                                        bringToFront = TRUE)
  ) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~SMR, opacity = 0.8,
            title = "SMR 2020 (observed/expected)", labFormat = labelFormat(digits = 2)) |>
  addControl(html = "<small>Data: JHU CSSE COVID-19 repository (Dong, Du &amp; Gardner 2020),
          deaths through 31 Dec 2020. Population: U.S. Census Bureau 2019.
          Boundaries: U.S. Census Bureau, 2020.</small>",
  position = "bottomleft")   # source line
```

::: callout-note
A `leaflet` map is an HTML widget: it appears in the rendered page on
your GitHub Pages site, which is where I grade it. It will not appear in
a PDF.
:::

## Part E --- Spatial weights and global Moran's I (4 points)

1.  Build a **queen contiguity** neighbour list. Report the average
    number of neighbours, the smallest and largest, and whether any
    county has none.
    Average number of neighbors: 5.1
    Smallest number of neighbors: 2
    Largest number of neighbors: 9
    No counties are alone, all counties have neighbors.
    
2.  Convert it to **row-standardized** spatial weights. One sentence:
    what does row standardization do to a county's neighbours, and what
    does the spatial lag of the SMR then represent?
   Row-standardization takes the county's weights (1 per neighbor) and divides them by the number of neighbors.  This makes it so the number of neighbors a county has does not pull the calculation as much.  The spatial lag of SMR is the average of the SMR of that particular counties neighbors and it does not matter how many neighbors that county has.
    
3.  Compute **global Moran's I** for the SMR by permutation with
    `moran.mc()` (999 simulations; set a seed), and plot the permutation
    distribution with the observed value marked. Report $I$, its
    expectation under the null hypothesis, $-1/(n-1)$, and the
    $p$-value. In three or four sentences: what exactly is the null
    hypothesis, how does the simulation test it, and is there a spatial
    signal in the SMRs?
    Moran's I is at 0.289, suggesting that places of high neighbor rates are located near other places of high neighbor rates.  The expectation under the null hypothesis is that SMRs are random across the counties and there is no spatial association, in this case the expected value is −0.015 (1/(67-1)).  The simulation shuffles the SMRs to different counties at random 99 times and shows a distribution of what the Moran's I's looked like compared to the actual Moran's I.  The p-value is significant at 0.001 and the Moran's I is far out on the tail of the histogram indicating that there is a spatial signal in the SMRs. 
    
4.  Draw the **Moran scatterplot**, with every county labelled and
    coloured by quadrant. Name two or three counties in the high--high
    quadrant and two or three in the low--low quadrant, say in one
    sentence what the slope of the fitted line is, and say in one
    sentence what Moran's I does **not** tell you about these counties.
    High-High Quadrant Counties:Juniata, Cambria, Huntingdon
    Low-Low Quadrant Counties: Forest, Clinton, McKean
    The slope of the fitted line is Moran's I which is 0.3, so a county whose SMR is 1 unit higher has neighbors whose average SMR is 0.3 higher.  The Moran's I does not explain which counties form the clusters, if a individual county's quadrant is statistically significant, or why the pattern in the data exists.
    
    

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: e-starter

# E1
nb <- poly2nb(pa_covid, queen = TRUE)
summary(nb)
card(nb) |> range() #gives range of # of neighbors
any(card(nb) == 0) #FALSE means none are alone

# E2
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

# E3 -- shuffle the SMRs across counties 999 times
set.seed(374)
mc <- moran.mc(pa_covid$SMR, lw, nsim = 999)
mc

-1 / (nrow(pa_covid) - 1)          # expectation under the null

hist(mc$res, breaks = 40, main = "Permutation distribution of I", xlab = "I")
abline(v = mc$statistic, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# E4 -- moran.plot() labels only influential points; build it in ggplot2
mp_df <- pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(lag_SMR = lag.listw(lw, SMR),          # mean SMR of neighbours
         quad = case_when(
           SMR >= mean(SMR) & lag_SMR >= mean(SMR) ~ "High-High",
           SMR <  mean(SMR) & lag_SMR <  mean(SMR) ~ "Low-Low",
           SMR >= mean(SMR) & lag_SMR <  mean(SMR) ~ "High-Low",
           TRUE                                    ~ "Low-High"))

ggplot(mp_df, aes(SMR, lag_SMR)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(mp_df$SMR), linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(mp_df$SMR), linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = quad), size = 2) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = NAME), size = 2.6, max.overlaps = Inf) +   # every county
  labs(x = "SMR (2020)", y = "Mean of Neighbors", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

table(mp_df$quad)
```
